EXTRA CLASS · AGES 2–5 · 15 CARDS · 48 WORDS

Look & Learn.

Fifteen picture cards, four words each, and one tiny move on every picture — point at the moon, waddle like a duck, balance like a flamingo. This is the school’s lightest class: no sequence, no worksheets, just looking, saying and a little moving, for children from two to five.

Start with card 01 ↓Cover first, then cards 01–15 in order.
HOW LOOK & LEARN WORKS

Look at the picture, say the word, do the move.

Every card is a sheet of four mini-cards, and every mini-card does the same three things: shows one big clear picture, names it in one word, and hands you a move — the little action pill in the middle. Look & Point. Move & Count. Smell & Describe. You read the move, your child does it, and the word rides along on the action. Nothing here needs reading, printing or setting up; the whole method fits in the gap between lunch and shoes.

One card a sitting is plenty, and the order below is simply the order the cards were drawn. Each word on each card has its own short page — what the word names, where your child already meets it and one way to try it today — so you can land straight on the word your child just pointed at. Five of the forty-eight words (duck, banana, carrot, grapes and strawberry) already have their own flashcard pages in the school’s library; their links lead there, because a word should live in one home, not two.

WHERE THIS CLASS FITS

Three classes grow into these cards.

Look & Learn collects first words from three places on the Learning Path. The animal words (duck, bird, dog, cat, bee, owl) began in Animals and Sounds for 2-Year-Olds — Class 11. The fruit-and-vegetable words (banana, carrot, grapes, strawberry, pear, lemon, tomato, pumpkin) grew out of Fruits & Vegetables — Class 22. And the sky-and-season words (moon, star, cloud, raindrop, sun, leaf, acorn) belong beside Science, Nature & Discovery — Class 31. If your child is working through any of those classes, these cards are the pocket version — and if you are only here to look and say, that is the whole point.

Ages are a guide, not a test. Two-year-olds point and name; four-year-olds describe and count. Both are doing it right.
